html:
Chichén Itzá was a great Maya city in the north of the Yucatán peninsula in Mexico, at its height from about 900 to 1100. Its name means "at the mouth of the well of the Itzá", after the Sacred Cenote, a natural sinkhole into which offerings and people were thrown.

As the southern cities of the Maya emptied in the 800s and 900s, Chichén Itzá rose to lead the north. Its buildings mix older Maya styles with new ones:

  • El Castillo, the stepped pyramid of the feathered serpent Kukulcán, where the equinox sun casts a serpent of shadow down the stairs;
  • the Great Ballcourt, the largest in Mesoamerica, for the rubber ballgame;
  • the Temple of the Warriors, with its rows of carved columns;
  • the round observatory called El Caracol.

Its close likeness to Tula in central Mexico still puzzles scholars: trade, conquest or shared fashion across the Mesoamerican world. Its power faded after about 1100, and Mayapán led the north until the 1400s, though pilgrims still came to the cenote when the Spanish arrived. The Dresden Codex was probably made in its region.
